speaker: Doctor
text: Can you describe the dizziness as spinning or just feeling lightheaded, and does it happen in specific situations like turning your head or standing up?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the detailed description. To narrow this down, do these episodes last only seconds, and is there any associated hearing loss or tinnitus in the affected ear? REQUEST TEST: Audiometry

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Audiometry: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with presbycusis. No sudden drops in hearing indicative of Meniere’s disease or labyrinthitis.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, or recent respiratory infections. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). While a previous provider suggested migraine, the strictly positional nature of the vertigo without auditory symptoms or headache strongly points to canalolithiasis; I recommend a Dix-Hallpike maneuver confirmation.
